outline.description: Introduces the parties, the marks at issue, the nature of the services, and the path from USPTO examination through TTAB opposition to the Federal Circuit appeal.
subtopics: Parties and marks: CC Serve’s ASPIRE word mark (Reg. No. 2126948; priority October 17, 1996) for credit card services; Apex Bank’s intent-to-use ASPIRE BANK word and design marks

Nature of services: CC Serve partners with banks to issue ASPIRE-branded credit cards and services the accounts; Apex is a Tennessee retail bank offering deposit accounts and loans, not credit cards, planning an internet bank under ASPIRE BANK
Prosecution history: Apex’s August 2019 ITU applications for “banking and financing services”; CC Serve’s letter of protest; examining attorney’s approval; publication on December 17, 2019
TTAB opposition: CC Serve’s Section 2(d) opposition; Board sustains likelihood of confusion and refuses registration
Appeal and jurisdiction: Apex appeals to the Federal Circuit; jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1295(a)(4)(B)

outline.chapter_title: Governing Law and Standards of Review
outline.description: Sets out the Section 2(d) likelihood-of-confusion framework, the DuPont factors, and the Federal Circuit’s standards for reviewing TTAB decisions.
subtopics: Section 2(d) of the Lanham Act: refusal when concurrent use would likely cause confusion
The DuPont factors: thirteen, with the Board considering only those relevant and of record
Standard of review: legal conclusions de novo; factual findings for substantial evidence (relevant evidence a reasonable mind could accept)
Nature of the inquiry: likelihood of confusion is a legal question based on underlying factual findings on each factor
Key precedents cited: DuPont; M2 Software; Bose; Coach Services

outline.chapter_title: Factor Two: Similarity of the Services—Affirmance
outline.description: Explains why the Board’s finding that the parties’ services are highly similar (and legally identical in part) was supported by substantial evidence and affirmed.
subtopics: Board’s task: compare CC Serve’s “credit card services” to Apex’s “banking and financing services”

Defining the identified services: despite deletion of “credit card services” from the ID Manual, Board interprets it to include issuing cards, counseling on card debt, processing and authorization, monitoring/alerts, account management, access to credit scores
Dictionary definitions: “bank,” “banking,” and “finance” encompass extending credit, including via credit cards
Third-party registrations: evidence that single sources commonly offer both credit card and broader banking/financing services under one mark
Board’s conclusion: services are highly similar and legally identical in part; factor two weighs heavily for CC Serve

Apex’s arguments and rejection: services are not the same or directly competitive; CC Serve is not a bank—Federal Circuit holds substantial evidence supports the Board’s similarity finding; affirmance of factor two

outline.chapter_title: Factor Six: Number and Nature of Similar Marks—Error and Remand
outline.description: Analyzes the Board’s treatment of third-party ‘Aspire’ uses, explains the legal error in narrowing the relevant universe, and sets out the Federal Circuit’s instructions on remand.
subtopics: Purpose of factor six: crowded-field evidence bears on commercial strength and scope of protection (Palm Bay; Juice Generation; Jack Wolfskin)
Apex’s evidence: multiple third-party ‘Aspire’ and ‘Aspire’-formative uses in credit card-related and broader financial services

Board’s approach: limited relevant public to “consumers of credit card services,” treated ‘Aspire’ uses for other banking/financing services as essentially irrelevant; found only nine relevant uses and deemed them insufficient to show weakness; concluded ASPIRE gets the normal scope of protection

Federal Circuit’s legal correction: factor six concerns similar, not identical, goods/services (Olde Tyme Foods; Juice Generation); when factor two found services highly similar and partly legally identical, the same scope of similarity must inform factor six
Holding on factor six: vacated; remanded for reconsideration of third-party marks across the full range of similar banking and financing services consistent with the factor two similarity finding

outline.chapter_title: Factor One: Similarity of the Marks, Disposition, and Significance
outline.description: Explains why the Board’s factor-one analysis must be revisited in light of factor six, states the court’s disposition, and identifies key takeaways for trademark practice.
subtopics: Factor one framework: appearance, sound, connotation, and commercial impression (I.AM.Symbolic)
Interdependence with factor six: commercial strength or weakness shapes commercial impression; reassessment of crowded-field evidence may alter the factor-one analysis
Disposition: affirm the Board on factor two; vacate on factors six and one; remand for reconsideration consistent with the services’ high similarity; costs to appellant

Practical significance: maintain consistent scope of “similarity” across DuPont factors; factor six does not require identical goods; robust third-party use in related financial services can narrow scope of protection and influence commercial impression
